rules.text: A function either orders the steps of a task or carries out one of them. The orchestration (the order of the calls and the control flow) does not share a function with the rules of the domain and the I/O; it calls named units that hold them.

question.instructions: Read each function of the file. Is there a function that decides the order of the steps of a task (calls, control flow) and also computes a rule of the domain and does the I/O of those steps itself? A function that only orders calls, one that carries out one step, and a file with no function or with only classes that declare data do not break the rule. A log call is not I/O. An entry point that reads its arguments, calls the steps, prints a summary and returns an exit code, and the loop of a transport that reads a message, dispatches it and writes the reply, only order calls.

criteria.true: a function mixes the order of the steps with the logic and the I/O of those steps
criteria.false: orchestration and the steps it calls live in separate functions, or the file declares data only

rules.text: Layers and packages are named `entrypoints`, `api`, `database`, `impl` and `core`, an interface is a port and its implementation an adapter, and a concept that already has a name gets no synonym.

question.instructions: Read the names of the modules, packages, classes and functions that the file defines or imports from the project. Answer true only when one of those units is named with a synonym of a term of the house vocabulary (layers entrypoints, api, database, impl, core; ports and adapters), such as manager, handler, helper, processor, common, shared, persistence or dal. These do not count: a word inside a string or in data, a local variable, a name imported from a library (`APILogHandler`, structlog `Processor`), a name of the domain, and folders inside a layer such as routers, schemas, requests, responses, tests or fakes.

criteria.true: a unit is named with a synonym of a term the vocabulary already has
criteria.false: no unit is named with a synonym of the vocabulary

rules.text: An access token that the server issues expires. Its lifetime is a number of seconds that the settings read from `ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`, after the prefix of the settings if they have one, with a short default, such as 900, when the variable is not set. Each project sets its own value. A session that lasts longer is kept by a refresh token that the server stores and replaces each time it is used. A judgment rule, a warning, for Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go and Rust.

question.instructions: Read the code that issues tokens in the file: the call that signs a token and the expiry it sets (`exp`, `expiresIn`, `setExpirationTime`, `ExpiresAt`). An access token is a token that authorizes requests on its own. Its lifetime should be a number of seconds that a setting reads from the variable `ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS` (after a prefix of the settings, such as `APP_`), with a short default such as 900; the value that a project sets is its own choice. Is an access token issued with no expiry, with an expiry that a setting can turn off (`None` or `0` meaning no expiry), or with a lifetime written in the code instead of read from the settings? A refresh token that the server stores and replaces at each use, and a token that the file only verifies, do not break the rule.

criteria.true: an access token is issued with no expiry, with an expiry that can be turned off, or with a lifetime written in the code
criteria.false: each access token issued in the file expires after a lifetime read from the settings, or the file issues no access token

rules.text: Tests drive the logic through in-memory adapters of the ports of the project: working fakes that implement the same interface as the production adapter. A mock stands in only for a third-party boundary that cannot reasonably be faked. `botica refs show in-memory-adapters` prints an adapter with its port.

question.instructions: Read the tests of the file. Does a test replace a port of the project with a mock, or assert on the calls that a mock received, where a working in-memory adapter of the port would drive the logic? A mock of a third-party boundary that cannot reasonably be faked does not break the rule.

criteria.true: the tests mock a port of the project, or assert on the calls a mock received
criteria.false: the tests use in-memory adapters of the ports and assert on outcomes

rules.text: Tests call the unit under test through the public interface that production code calls, and assert on observable behaviour. A test reads no private attribute, calls no underscore-prefixed member and asserts on no internal state of the unit.

question.instructions: Read the tests of the file. Does a test read a private attribute of the unit under test, call one of its underscore-prefixed members, or assert on its internal state instead of on what its public interface returns or does? A name with an underscore that the test file defines itself, and loading the module under test from its path, do not break the rule.

criteria.true: a test reaches into private attributes, private methods or internal state of the unit under test
criteria.false: the tests call the public interface and assert on observable behaviour

rules.text: Prose says what a thing is and what it does, in plain sentences that a file, a command or an issue of the repository backs, with no inflated words, hedges, trailing judgments, bold emphasis or claims without a source.

question.instructions: Read the prose of the file. Does it carry a sign of model writing: inflated significance, a trailing clause that judges, words that avoid is and has, definition by negation, a sentence that strings three items for rhythm, hedges and vague attribution, bold for emphasis, text addressed to the reader, or a claim with no source? Commands, code, lists of names and a bulleted list of cases are not prose, and the bold label at the start of each decision or option of an ADR is not bold for emphasis.

criteria.true: the prose carries one or more of the signs
criteria.false: the prose is plain and carries none of the signs

rules.text: A comment says only what the code cannot say through its names and its structure: the reason for a choice that looks wrong, an invariant, a workaround with the link to its cause, or the docstring of a public interface.

question.instructions: Read the comments of the file and the code next to them. Leave out first the comments that never break the rule: a comment whose text starts with `MARK:`, which botica and editors read as the start of a section; a header that describes the whole file; a doc comment or docstring of any item; the code of a standard cited alone; a directive that a tool reads (a suppression, `zizmor: ignore`, `noqa`); and an option of a template left commented out under a comment that says how to turn it on. Of the comments left, does one repeat what the next lines say, name a section of the file, keep code commented out or tell the history of a change? A comment that gives the reason for a choice that looks wrong, an invariant the types do not show or a workaround with the link to its cause does not break the rule, however many such comments the file has. Attributes such as `#[test]` are not comments. A file with no comment left does not break the rule.

criteria.true: a comment repeats the code, names a section, keeps old code or tells the history of a change
criteria.false: every comment says something the code cannot, or the file has none

rules.text: Each concept of the domain has one term, the one that `GLOSSARY.md` defines, in the code and in the documentation. `GLOSSARY.md` lists each term with its definition and the words to avoid for it, and the code and the documentation use the term.

question.instructions: Read the names and the prose of the file. Does it give one concept of the domain two or more names, such as a parameter `client` of type `Customer` next to an `account` of the same type, or a name that the glossary of the project (GLOSSARY.md) says to avoid, when the glossary is in view? Terms of programming and names of a library are not terms of the domain. A document that shows a violation as an example, such as the `Don't` section of a rule, does not commit it.

criteria.true: a concept has two names, or a name the glossary says to avoid
criteria.false: each concept has one term, the one of the glossary
